transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-10-29
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration approx: 58 minutes
Attendees: Maya Lopez (Redwood AE), Ethan Ross (Redwood SE), John Keller (CTO, Nimbus), Sara Ahmed (Head of AI/ML, Nimbus), Raj Patel (Security Architect, Nimbus)

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Maya from Redwood, I'm the AE on this account, and with me is Ethan, our solutions engineer. How's everyone doing?
[00:08] John: Good, thanks. Good to meet you both.
[00:10] Sara: Hi, thanks.
[00:12] Maya: Quick agenda — we want to understand your constraints for an on-prem air-gapped deployment, walk through our typical offline update flows, hardware requirements, and then next steps for a pilot. Is that right on your side?
[00:22] Raj: Yep, that's right. We're primarily focused on security and operational model updates without any outbound network.
[00:27] Ethan: Okay great. To start, can you give us a quick picture of your environment — physical data center, GPU types, orchestration?
[00:35] John: Sure. We run two colo sites, completely isolated from public internet. We have custom racks, currently filled with a mix of NVIDIA A100 80GB and a few H100s on the older side. We do use on-prem Kubernetes but it's heavily locked down — air-gapped cluster, no outbound, only internal registry mirrors.
[00:50] Ethan: Got it. For an on-prem Redwood Private deployment we typically support k8s-based installs or our appliance model. In air-gapped installs we provide an offline bundle for the control plane and model artifacts — it's basically a tarball you bring in via secure media. We sign models and provide checksums.
[01:10] Sara: How do you handle model upgrades? We can't have automatic pulls from public clouds.
[01:14] Ethan: We have an offline update process: Redwood prepares a signed update package containing the model weights, runtime images, and migrations. Your security team verifies the signature using the public key we provide, and then the package is applied using your approved change window. For high assurance, we can support hardware HSM to verify sigs on-device.
[01:31] Raj: We need to see the signature verification flow and how it ties to our HSM. Also, what's the size of these model bundles? We're sensitive to transfer windows.
[01:40] Ethan: Model bundle sizes depend on quantization — a full fp16 Llama-style can be hundreds of GBs, quantized 4-bit variants are smaller. For example, a 70B in 4-bit can be ~40-60GB compressed. We'll provide a sizing spreadsheet. For transfer, we recommend a staged approach: initial model load via encrypted external drive, then incremental delta patches for smaller updates.
[01:58] John: Delta patches — do you do binary diffs or whole model replaces?
[02:02] Ethan: Mostly whole artifacts for model changes, but for runtime patches we do smaller container deltas. We're exploring differential weight patches, but that's not explicitly productionized across all architectures yet — it's model dependent.
[02:15] Sara: What's the runtime — do you require specific NVIDIA driver versions or CUDA toolkits? We're on a curated image stack, upgrades are slow.
[02:22] Ethan: We document supported driver/CUDA combos per model and per runtime. For H100/A100: we recommend NVIDIA driver 535+ and CUDA 12.x for best perf, but we can support older stacks with caveats. We'll include an explicit compatibility matrix in the runbook.
[02:38] Raj: And encryption at rest / key management — we require integration with our HSM and local KMS. How does Redwood handle keys?
[02:45] Ethan: Redwood Private lets you bring your own KMS. For air-gapped installs, we support an HSM-based key wrap workflow — keys never leave your HSM. Our control plane integrates with a KMS connector that speaks to your HSM over the internal network. We also emit audit logs for every key operation.
[03:02] John: Audit logs — retention policies? We need immutable logs for 7 years for some workflows.
[03:08] Maya: We can export logs to your SIEM and support append-only storage. We'll need to map out retention requirements and secure archival.
[03:15] Raj: Also SOC2 and ISO certifications — we need to see evidence and previous pen test results.
[03:20] Maya: Absolutely, we'll send the security packet after this call (SOC2, ISO docs, and pen test summaries).
[03:26] Sara: Network side, we have strict egress rules; any agent that phone-homes is a non-starter. Does your control plane require outbound verification?
[03:34] Ethan: For air-gapped, no outbound required — the control plane runs locally. We do recommend a scheduled validation process you can run manually to verify package signatures, but it's a pull-by-admin process, not automatic outbound.
[03:45] John: What about telemetry and metrics? We need both operational metrics and token-level cost logs for internal chargeback but we can't send telemetry offsite.
[03:54] Ethan: We can run the observability stack fully on-prem. There's a toggle in the install to disable outbound telemetry. We can also provide an encrypted usage export you can periodically review or ship to us under NDA if you need managed support.
[04:10] Sara: On the topic of model provenance — do you support pinned model versions and reproducible builds? We need to be able to roll back to a known-good version quickly.
[04:17] Ethan: Yes. The platform supports model version pinning and can do canary rollouts within your private cluster. Rollout control is admin initiated. Rollbacks are supported and we retain previous artifact signatures for verification.
[04:29] Raj: Any concerns about hardware topology? We have nodes with NVLink in some racks and not others. Latency for key-value cache across nodes bothers us for real-time inference.
[04:40] Ethan: Our runtime supports intra-node KV cache optimizations and we can recommend model sharding strategies. For low-latency needs we recommend colocating GPU nodes with low-latency interconnects for hot endpoints, and using caching strategies for prefix reuse. We'll include guidance in the runbook.
[04:58] John: From an ops perspective, how much hands-on from Redwood is required for initial install? We try to minimize vendor people on site due to compliance.
[05:05] Maya: We do remote-led installs usually, but for air-gapped customers we often propose a 2-day onsite knowledge transfer. If you prefer no vendor personnel onsite, we can do a fully remote install with step-by-step signed runbook and white-glove support via your infra team.
[05:21] Raj: What about vulnerability patching for the runtime? Will we get signed patches and a CVE list?
[05:26] Ethan: Yes, patches are packaged and signed. We publish a CVE tracker for runtime components and can provide patch advisories with risk classification. Patches are applied in scheduled maintenance windows you control.
[05:38] Sara: Can you comment on model licensing — if we want to use an open model and then fine-tune, are there any extra restrictions?
[05:45] Maya: License depends on upstream model. We curate a model catalog and annotate licensing. For fine-tuning, we can host your trained artifact on-prem. We'll include a note in the runbook about acceptable model licenses.
[05:56] John: Timeline wise — if we do a pilot, what's typical? Four-to-six weeks?
[06:00] Ethan: A basic pilot to validate inference and offline update workflow is commonly 4 weeks: week 0 install prep and hardware validation, week 1 install and baseline benchmarks, week 2 workload testing and security review, week 3 wrap-up and runbook handoff.
[06:14] Raj: Price gating — we have to build a business case for reserved capacity. We'll need sample pricing for a pilot and for dedicated monthly commitments.
[06:21] Maya: We'll include pilot pricing options and Dedicated capacity quotes in the follow-up.
[06:25] [long silence / cross-talk while someone pulls diagrams]
[06:40] Sara: One more question — how does Redwood handle failover if a model node becomes compromised or is offline? Does the system fail open to a hosted endpoint?
[06:48] Ethan: We support configured fallbacks. In air-gapped customers we generally don't allow automatic outbound fallbacks. Instead we recommend local warm standby nodes or a policy to fail to a smaller local model variant. If you want automatic cloud fallback, that requires an explicit outbound allowance and additional approvals.
[07:05] John: We won't allow egress, so fallbacks will be local-only.
[07:09] Maya: That's fine, we can design for local redundancy.
[07:12] [summary recap]
[07:15] Maya: Quick recap — action items: we will send security packet and runbook, Ethan will prepare hardware checklist and offline update diagram, Nimbus to share network diagram. We'll prepare pilot pricing. Any objections?
[07:25] Raj: No objections. Looks good.
[07:27] Sara: Sounds good.
[07:28] John: Thanks, looking forward to the materials.
[07:30] Maya: Great, we'll follow up by email with attachments and a proposed pilot schedule. Thanks everyone.

Notes on transcription quality: fairly accurate but some product names and exact version numbers may be mis-transcribed. References to KV cache sometimes hyphenated in the capture.
